claims.statement: Kumanokusubi is a deity in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Kumanokusubi adalah dewa dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: Kumanokusubi (熊野久须毘命,熊野櫲樟日命, Wonder Worker of Bear Moors) is a God in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: The tradition counts him as Amaterasu’s fifth son.
claims.statement_id: Tradisi menghitungnya sebagai putra kelima Amaterasu.
claims.quote: He is the fifth son of Amaterasu.

claims.statement: His birth belongs to a contest between Amaterasu and Susanoo.
claims.statement_id: Kelahirannya merupakan bagian dari perlombaan antara Amaterasu dan Susanoo.
claims.quote: He was born out of a kami-making competition between Amaterasu and Susanoo.

claims.statement: One version describes five male kami arising from chewed beads.
claims.statement_id: Satu versi menggambarkan lima kami laki-laki lahir dari manik-manik yang dikunyah.
claims.quote: In many versions, Susanoo took Amaterasu's beads and crushed them within his mouth, which created five male kami.

claims.statement: The Kojiki connects his emergence with the jeweled cord on Amaterasu’s right wrist.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menghubungkan kemunculannya dengan untaian permata di pergelangan kanan Amaterasu.
claims.quote: Then he asked for the jeweled [cord] adorning her right wrist, and [she] handed it over [to him]. He chewed it up and spat the bits out in a misty spray from which a deity named Kumanokusubi no mikoto 熊野久湏毗命 came into existence (15).

claims.statement: The birth narrative describes the chewed material being spat out as a misty spray.
claims.statement_id: Narasi kelahiran menggambarkan bahan yang dikunyah diludahkan sebagai semburan berkabut.
claims.quote: Then he asked for the jeweled [cord] adorning her right wrist, and [she] handed it over [to him]. He chewed it up and spat the bits out in a misty spray from which a deity named Kumanokusubi no mikoto 熊野久湏毗命 came into existence (15).

claims.statement: It is described as partly human and partly animal.
claims.statement_id: Ia digambarkan sebagai makhluk setengah manusia dan setengah hewan.

claims.statement_id: Satu penjelasan menghubungkan namanya dengan istilah Jepang mizuchi.
claims.quote: The Ainu word mintuci is considered to be borrowed from the Japanese word mizuchi (or variants thereof), that are local appellations for the kappa, ultimately deriving from the term mizuchi, which signifies a type of dragon.

claims.statement_id: Mishaguji adalah sebutan kelompok kami yang dihormati di wilayah Suwa.

claims.statement: They were important in winter and spring shrine ceremonies.
claims.statement_id: Mereka berperan penting dalam upacara kuil pada musim dingin dan musim semi.
claims.quote: These spirits once played a key role in the shrine’s winter and spring religious ceremonies and are also enshrined in numerous smaller shrines throughout the region.

claims.statement: A ritual priest was said to summon them into people or objects.

claims.quote: In these ceremonies, the Kan-no-Osa or Jinchō (神長) — also known as Jinchōkan (神長官) — a high-ranking ritual priest from the Moriya clan, would summon the Mishaguji into vessels (yorishiro), such as individuals or objects, to be temporarily inhabited during the rite.

claims.statement: The rites concluded with a formal dismissal of the spirits.
claims.statement_id: Ritual itu diakhiri dengan pelepasan roh secara resmi.
claims.quote: Upon completion, the spirits were ritually dismissed.

claims.quote: It is said to be chief among all shelled creatures.

claims.statement: It belongs to the Four Intelligent Beasts.
claims.statement_id: Ia termasuk dalam Empat Hewan Cerdas.
claims.quote: Among the Four Intelligent Beasts (四靈), a list of auspicious animals, the turtle goes by several names.

claims.statement: The Shuyiji calls a turtle older than ten thousand years spiritual.
claims.statement_id: Shuyiji menyebut kura-kura yang berusia lebih dari sepuluh ribu tahun sebagai kura-kura roh.
claims.quote: According to the Shuyiji (述異記 Tales of Strange Matters) compiled by Ren Fang, a turtle that has lived for one thousand years has grown hair, a five thousand year old tortoise is called a "divine turtle" (神龜) and an animal older than ten thousand years is called a "spiritual turtle" (靈龜).

claims.statement: The Baopuzi instead describes a thousand-year-old spirit turtle.
claims.statement_id: Baopuzi justru menggambarkan kura-kura roh berusia seribu tahun.
claims.quote: The Baopuzi gives a slightly different account, describing the spirit turtle as one thousand years old.

claims.statement: Sunekosuri is a Japanese yōkai whose name refers to rubbing against legs.
claims.statement_id: Sunekosuri adalah yōkai Jepang yang namanya merujuk pada gesekan pada kaki.
claims.quote: The sunekosuri (meaning "rub against lower legs") is a Japanese yōkai.

claims.statement: Okayama tales describe it obstructing pedestrians.
claims.statement_id: Cerita Okayama menggambarkannya menghalangi pejalan kaki.
claims.quote: Stories are told of it in Okayama Prefecture and is said to get in the way of people's paths as they walk.

claims.statement: One local account gives it a dog’s shape.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah setempat memberinya wujud anjing.
claims.quote: According to folklore from Ibara in Nankaichi town within this city, sunekosuri would appear beside a shrine called Iryō-dō, and it would move through the space between the legs of pedestrians and would take the shape of a dog.

claims.statement: It is said to appear on rainy nights in streets and alleys.
claims.statement_id: Ia konon muncul di jalan dan gang pada malam hujan.
claims.quote: They appear on rainy nights in streets and alleys where people travel.

claims.statement: Its movements between people’s legs make walking difficult.
claims.statement_id: Gerakannya di antara kaki manusia menyulitkan orang berjalan.
claims.quote: They rub against their shins, weave in and out of their legs, nuzzle against the knees, and otherwise make it difficult to walk.

claims.statement: It is not portrayed as deliberately harmful, though it can make people stumble.
claims.statement_id: Ia tidak digambarkan sengaja mencelakai, meskipun dapat membuat orang tersandung.
claims.quote: They do not intentionally cause any harm to humans, although occasionally their rubbing is strong enough to make a person stumble or even knock them down.

claims.statement: Ta-no-Kami is an agricultural kami associated with a good rice harvest.
claims.statement_id: Ta-no-Kami adalah kami pertanian yang dikaitkan dengan panen padi yang baik.
claims.quote: Ta-no-Kami (田の神) is a kami who is believed to observe the harvest of rice plants or to bring a good harvest, by Japanese farmers.

claims.statement: The element ta means rice fields.
claims.statement_id: Unsur ta berarti sawah.
claims.quote: Ta in Japanese means "rice fields".

claims.statement: Noushin is another designation used for the deity.
claims.statement_id: Noushin adalah sebutan lain yang dipakai untuk dewa itu.
claims.quote: Ta-no-Kami is also called Noushin (kami of agriculture) or kami of peasants.

claims.statement: Some southern Japanese communities pray before stone images.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian komunitas di Jepang selatan berdoa di hadapan patung batu.
claims.quote: Ta-no-Kami in Kagoshima Prefecture and parts of Miyazaki Prefecture is unique; farmers pray before Ta-no-Kami stone statues in their communities.

claims.statement: Farmers hold related ceremonies in spring and autumn.
claims.statement_id: Petani mengadakan upacara terkait pada musim semi dan musim gugur.
claims.quote: According to their agricultural calendars, farmers observe kami ceremonies related to Ta-no-Kami in the spring and autumn.

claims.statement: Prayers also seek protection from disasters and harmful insects.
claims.statement_id: Doa juga memohon perlindungan dari bencana dan serangga pengganggu.
claims.quote: They also pray for the elimination of disasters or harmful insects.

claims.statement: Toyokumono is a deity in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Toyokumono adalah dewa dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: 『古事記』では豊雲野神、『日本書紀』では豊斟渟尊（トヨクムヌ）と表記される。

claims.statement: The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki write the deity’s name differently.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki dan Nihon Shoki menuliskan nama dewa itu secara berbeda.
claims.quote: 『古事記』では豊雲野神、『日本書紀』では豊斟渟尊（トヨクムヌ）と表記される。

claims.statement: The Kojiki places the deity second in the Seven Generations.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menempatkan dewa itu pada urutan kedua dalam Tujuh Generasi.
claims.quote: 『古事記』において神世七代の第二代の神とされ、『日本書紀』では天地開闢に登場する神世七代の第三代の神とされる。また神世七代の最後の独神である。

claims.statement: The Nihon Shoki gives the deity third place in its opening account.
claims.statement_id: Nihon Shoki menempatkan dewa itu pada urutan ketiga dalam kisah pembukanya.
claims.quote: 『古事記』において神世七代の第二代の神とされ、『日本書紀』では天地開闢に登場する神世七代の第三代の神とされる。また神世七代の最後の独神である。

claims.statement: The Kojiki describes Toyokumono as a solitary deity.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menggambarkan Toyokumono sebagai dewa tunggal.
claims.quote: Next was Toyokumono no kami 豊雲野神 (2). These two deities also came into existence as solitary deities and hid their bodies.

claims.statement: That account says the deity hid its body.
claims.statement_id: Kisah tersebut menyebut dewa itu menyembunyikan tubuhnya.
claims.quote: Next was Toyokumono no kami 豊雲野神 (2). These two deities also came into existence as solitary deities and hid their bodies.

claims.statement: Tsurubebi is a fire yōkai depicted by Toriyama Sekien.
claims.statement_id: Tsurubebi adalah yōkai api yang digambar oleh Toriyama Sekien.
claims.quote: The tsurubebi (釣瓶火, "bucket fire") is a fire yōkai that appears in the Gazu Hyakki Yagyō by Toriyama Sekien.

claims.statement: The original illustration gives no explanatory text.
claims.statement_id: Ilustrasi aslinya tidak memberi keterangan.
claims.quote: The illustration does not give any explanatory text

claims.statement: One account portrays it as a nocturnal tree spirit in coniferous forests.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah menggambarkannya sebagai roh pohon malam hari di hutan konifer.
claims.quote: Tsurubebi are small tree spirits which appear at night, deep in coniferous forests.

claims.statement: It appears as bluish-white fire moving between branches and the ground.
claims.statement_id: Ia muncul sebagai api putih kebiruan yang bergerak antara cabang dan tanah.
claims.quote: They take the form of blueish-white orbs of fire which bob up and down in the branches, occasionally dropping to the forest floor and floating back up into the trees.

claims.statement: A human or animal face may be visible in its flames.
claims.statement_id: Wajah manusia atau hewan kadang terlihat di dalam apinya.
claims.quote: Sometimes the vague shape of a human or bestial face can be seen in the flames.

claims.statement: Its fire is described as producing no heat or damage to trees.
claims.statement_id: Apinya digambarkan tidak menghasilkan panas atau merusak pohon.
claims.quote: Their flames produce no heat and do not burn the trees that they live in; nor do these yokai pose any other known threat.

claims.statement: Umashiashikabihikoji is a Shinto deity.
claims.statement_id: Umashiashikabihikoji adalah dewa Shinto.
claims.quote: Umashiashikabihikoji (宇摩志阿斯訶備比古遅; Lit. "Elderly Prince Reed-Shoot") is a kami (Shinto deity).

claims.statement: The Kojiki places his emergence early in the universe’s creation.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menempatkan kemunculannya pada awal penciptaan alam semesta.
claims.quote: According to the Kojiki, he came into being as a hitorigami early in the creation of the universe.

claims.statement: He is counted as the fourth deity to emerge in that account.
claims.statement_id: Ia dihitung sebagai dewa keempat yang muncul dalam kisah tersebut.
claims.quote: He was the fourth kami to come into existence and the first to have a gendered name.

claims.statement: His origin is associated with something sprouting like a reed shoot.
claims.statement_id: Asalnya dikaitkan dengan sesuatu yang bertunas seperti pucuk gelagah.
claims.quote: a deity came into existence from a thing that sprouted forth like a reed shoot. Its name was Umashi ashikabi hikoji no kami 宇摩志阿斯訶備比古遅神 (8).

claims.statement: The narrative describes this early group as solitary deities who hide themselves.
claims.statement_id: Narasi menggambarkan kelompok awal ini sebagai dewa tunggal yang menyembunyikan diri.
claims.quote: These two deities also came into existence as solitary deities and hid their bodies. The five deities named above are the set-apart heavenly deities (10).

claims.statement: The Nihon Shoki preserves other orders of emergence for this deity.
claims.statement_id: Nihon Shoki menyimpan urutan kemunculan lain bagi dewa ini.
claims.quote: Umashiashikabihikoji also makes appearances in the Nihon Shoki, though there his name is Umashiashikabihikoji-no-mikoto (可美葦芽彦舅尊; Lit. "Sweet Elderly Prince Reed-Shoot") and there are several different stories, some of which claim he was the first kami, while others claim he was the second.

claims.statement: Wakumusubi is an agricultural kami.
claims.statement_id: Wakumusubi adalah kami pertanian.
claims.quote: Wakumusubi (和久産巣日神) is a kami of agriculture.

claims.statement: Several accounts describe his birth from Izanami’s urine.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa kisah menggambarkan kelahirannya dari urine Izanami.
claims.quote: In many versions, he was born from the urine of Izanami when she died.

claims.statement: A Nihon Shoki version instead makes him the child of Kagutsuchi and Haniyasu-hime.
claims.statement_id: Versi Nihon Shoki justru menjadikannya anak Kagutsuchi dan Haniyasu-hime.
claims.quote: Another version of the Nihon Shoki states he was a child of Kagutsuchi and Haniyasu-hime.

claims.statement: He is enshrined at Aiki Jinja.
claims.statement_id: Ia dipuja di Aiki Jinja.
claims.quote: He is enshrined at Aiki Jinja.

claims.statement: He is described as Mizuhanome’s brother.
claims.statement_id: Ia digambarkan sebagai saudara laki-laki Mizuhanome.
claims.quote: He is the brother of Mizuhanome.

claims.statement: The Kojiki identifies Toyoukebime as his child.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menyebut Toyoukebime sebagai anaknya.
claims.quote: Next [appeared] Wakumusuhi no kami 和久産巣日神 (6). The child of this deity is called Toyoukebime no kami 豊宇気毗売神 (7).

claims.statement: Yosuzume are bird yōkai known as night sparrows.
claims.statement_id: Yosuzume adalah yōkai burung yang disebut burung pipit malam.
claims.quote: Yosuzume (夜雀, "Night-Sparrow") are bird yōkai

claims.statement: They appear at night and chirp like sparrows on mountain trails.
claims.statement_id: Mereka muncul malam hari dan berkicau seperti burung pipit di jalur pegunungan.
claims.quote: As indicated by their name, they are a yōkai that appear in the night and chirp "chi, chi, chi" like a sparrow, and are said to pass in front of people who walk along mountain trails.

claims.statement: One belief says catching them causes night blindness.
claims.statement_id: Satu kepercayaan menyebut penangkapan burung itu menyebabkan rabun senja.
claims.quote: Also, it is said that if one carelessly caught them, then one gets afflicted with nyctalopia.

claims.statement: In Wakayama, their presence can indicate a protective wolf.
claims.statement_id: Di Wakayama, keberadaannya dapat menandakan serigala pelindung.
claims.quote: In reverse, in Wakayama Prefecture, they were not bad luck, and while possessed by a night sparrow, it was proof that a wolf was giving protection from the monsters of the mountain.

claims.statement: Other accounts interpret their presence as bad luck.
claims.statement_id: Kisah lain menafsirkan keberadaan mereka sebagai pertanda sial.
claims.quote: By themselves they don’t do any particular harm other than startling people; however they are a sign of very bad luck and are thought to bring terrible evil to those whom they swarm around.

claims.statement: A regional account says only one traveler in a group hears their call.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah daerah menyebut hanya satu pelancong dalam kelompok yang mendengar suaranya.
claims.quote: Their call is mysteriously only ever heard by a single individual, even when traveling in groups.

claims.statement: The Kojiki makes her the wife of Amenohiboko, a Silla prince.

claims.statement: A story describes a red jewel becoming a beautiful maiden.
claims.statement_id: Satu cerita menggambarkan permata merah berubah menjadi perempuan muda yang cantik.
claims.quote: 男が釈明をしても天之日矛は許さなかったので、男はいつも持ち歩いていた赤い玉を差し出して、ようやく許してもらえた。天之日矛がその玉を持ち帰って床に置くと、玉は美しい娘になった。

claims.statement: After her husband insults her, she escapes by boat to Naniwa.
claims.statement_id: Setelah suaminya menghinanya, ia melarikan diri dengan perahu ke Naniwa.

claims.quote: しかし、ある日奢り高ぶった天之日矛が妻を罵ったので、親の国に帰ると言って小舟に乗って難波の津に逃げてきた。その娘は、難波の比売碁曾の社に鎮まる阿加流比売神であるという。

claims.statement: Ame-no-Fuyukinu is a figure in Japanese divine genealogy.
claims.statement_id: Ame-no-Fuyukinu adalah sosok dalam silsilah dewa Jepang.
claims.quote: Ame-no-Fuyukinu (Japanese: 天之冬衣神) is a figure of Japanese legend said to be a fifth generation descendent of Susanoo, married to Sashikuniwaka-hime, and father of Ōkuninushi.

claims.statement: He is described as a fifth-generation descendant of Susanoo.
claims.statement_id: Ia digambarkan sebagai keturunan generasi kelima Susanoo.
claims.quote: Ame-no-Fuyukinu (Japanese: 天之冬衣神) is a figure of Japanese legend said to be a fifth generation descendent of Susanoo, married to Sashikuniwaka-hime, and father of Ōkuninushi.

claims.statement: His wife is named Sashikuniwaka-hime.
claims.statement_id: Istrinya bernama Sashikuniwaka-hime.
claims.quote: Ame-no-Fuyukinu (Japanese: 天之冬衣神) is a figure of Japanese legend said to be a fifth generation descendent of Susanoo, married to Sashikuniwaka-hime, and father of Ōkuninushi.

claims.statement: He is identified as Ōkuninushi’s father.
claims.statement_id: Ia disebut sebagai ayah Ōkuninushi.
claims.quote: Ame-no-Fuyukinu (Japanese: 天之冬衣神) is a figure of Japanese legend said to be a fifth generation descendent of Susanoo, married to Sashikuniwaka-hime, and father of Ōkuninushi.

claims.statement: A legend has Susanoo order him to deliver a sword to Takamagahara.
claims.statement_id: Satu legenda menyebut Susanoo memerintahkannya membawa pedang ke Takamagahara.
claims.quote: Legend has it that Susanoo ordered him to deliver a sword to Takamagahara and that he founded Hinomisaki Shrine, while the Ono clan claim descent from him.

claims.statement: He is credited with founding Hinomisaki Shrine.
claims.statement_id: Ia dianggap sebagai pendiri Kuil Hinomisaki.
claims.quote: Legend has it that Susanoo ordered him to deliver a sword to Takamagahara and that he founded Hinomisaki Shrine, while the Ono clan claim descent from him.

claims.statement: Ame-no-Torifune is associated with a deity or divine vessel in Japanese myth.
claims.statement_id: Ame-no-Torifune dikaitkan dengan dewa atau kapal ilahi dalam mitos Jepang.
claims.quote: 鳥之石楠船神（トリノイワクスフネノカミ、歴史的仮名遣：トリノイハクスフネノカミ）は、日本神話に登場する神、または神が乗る船の名前である。

claims.statement: Ame-no-Torifune is an alternate name of Tori-no-Iwakusufune.
claims.statement_id: Ame-no-Torifune adalah nama lain Tori-no-Iwakusufune.
claims.quote: 別名を天鳥船神（あめのとりふねのかみ）、天鳥船（あめのとりふね）と言い、天夷鳥命と同神とする系図がある。

claims.statement: The Kojiki places the deity among the offspring of Izanaki and Izanami.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menempatkan dewa itu di antara anak Izanaki dan Izanami.
claims.quote: Next [Izanaki and Izanami] gave birth to a deity whose name is Tori no iwakusufune no kami 鳥之石楠舩神. [This deity’s] other name is Ame no torifune 天鳥舩 (26).

claims.statement: The Kojiki sends the deity as Takemikazuchi’s companion in the land-transfer mission.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki mengirim dewa itu sebagai pendamping Takemikazuchi dalam misi penyerahan negeri.
claims.quote: 『古事記』の葦原中国平定の段では、天鳥船神が建御雷神の副使として葦原中国に派遣され、事代主神の意見をきくために使者として遣わされた。

claims.statement: The deity also serves as messenger to Kotoshironushi.
claims.statement_id: Dewa itu juga menjadi utusan kepada Kotoshironushi.
claims.quote: 『古事記』の葦原中国平定の段では、天鳥船神が建御雷神の副使として葦原中国に派遣され、事代主神の意見をきくために使者として遣わされた。

claims.statement: An academic commentary interprets the deity as a personification of ships.
claims.statement_id: Komentar akademik menafsirkan dewa itu sebagai personifikasi kapal.
claims.quote: The names of this deity indicate that it is a deification of ships.

claims.statement: Amenotokotachi is one of the primordial heavenly deities in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Amenotokotachi adalah salah satu dewa langit awal dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: 天之常立神（アメノトコタチ）は、日本神話に登場する神。別天津神のうちの一柱である。

claims.statement: The Kojiki places this deity last among the first five heavenly deities.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menempatkan dewa ini terakhir di antara lima dewa langit pertama.
claims.quote: 天地開闢の際、別天津神五柱の最後に現れた神である。独神であり、現れてすぐに身を隠した。

claims.statement: The early narrative describes Amenotokotachi as a solitary deity.
claims.statement_id: Narasi awal menggambarkan Amenotokotachi sebagai dewa tunggal.
claims.quote: Next Ame no tokotachi no kami 天之常立神 (9) [appeared]. These two deities also came into existence as solitary deities and hid their bodies.

claims.statement: That narrative says the deity hid its body.
claims.statement_id: Narasi tersebut menyebut dewa itu menyembunyikan tubuhnya.

claims.statement_id: Ia konon mengintai di gang dan kamar mandi.
claims.quote: They stalk alleys, bathrooms, or other out of the way places.

claims.statement: Kamotaketsunumi is a deity in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Kamotaketsunumi adalah dewa dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: Kamotaketsunumi no Mikoto (賀茂建角身命) is a god in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: He is identified with Yatagarasu.
claims.statement_id: Ia disamakan dengan Yatagarasu.
claims.quote: He is also known by the name Yatagarasu.

claims.statement: He is regarded as the ancestral founder of the Kamo clan.
claims.statement_id: Ia dianggap sebagai leluhur pendiri klan Kamo.
claims.quote: Kamotaketsunumi He is the founder of the Kamo clan of Yamashiro Province, and is known as the deity of the Shimogamo Shrine (Shimogamo Shrine).

claims.statement: The Shinsen Shōjiroku makes him Kamimusubi’s grandson.
claims.statement_id: Shinsen Shōjiroku menjadikannya cucu Kamimusubi.
claims.quote: According to Shinsen Shōjiroku, Kamotaketsunumi no Mikoto is the grandson of Kamimusubi.

claims.statement: A narrative has him take the form of Yatagarasu and guide Emperor Jimmu.
claims.statement_id: Satu narasi menyebutnya mengambil wujud Yatagarasu dan membimbing Kaisar Jimmu.
claims.quote: Kamotaketsunumi, under the command of Takamimusubi and Amaterasu, descended from the sky to the peak of Tsune in Hyuga and reached Mount Katsuragi in Yamato, where he incarnated as Yatagarasu and led Emperor Jimmu and contributed to his victory.

claims.statement: His children are named Tamayorihiko and Tamayorihime.
claims.statement_id: Anak-anaknya bernama Tamayorihiko dan Tamayorihime.
claims.quote: Kamotaketsunumi-no-Mikoto had two children, son Tamayorihiko-no-mikoto and daughter Tamayorihime-no-mikoto.

claims.statement: Kanayamahiko is a deity in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Kanayamahiko adalah dewa dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: 金山彦神（かなやまひこのかみ）は、日本神話に登場する神である。天津国玉神の父という説がある。

claims.statement: He is paired with the goddess Kanayamahime.
claims.statement_id: Ia dipasangkan dengan dewi Kanayamahime.
claims.quote: 『古事記』では金山毘古神、『日本書紀』では金山彦神と表記する。金山毘売神（かなやまびめのかみ、金山姫神）と対偶をなす神である。

claims.statement: The pair is interpreted as deities of mines.
claims.statement_id: Pasangan itu ditafsirkan sebagai dewa pertambangan.
claims.quote: 「金山」は鉱山と解するのが一般的で、金山毘古神・金山毘売神の二神は鉱山の神と解釈される。

claims.statement: The Kojiki has Kanayamahiko emerge from Izanami’s vomit.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menyebut Kanayamahiko muncul dari muntahan Izanami.
claims.quote: From her vomit (2) was born a deity named Kanayamabiko no kami 金山毗古神. Next [appeared] Kanayamabime no kami 金山毗売神 (3).

claims.statement: His birth follows Izanami’s injuries from bearing Kagutsuchi.
claims.statement_id: Kelahirannya terjadi setelah Izanami terluka akibat melahirkan Kagutsuchi.
claims.quote: 神産みにおいて、イザナミが火の神カグツチを産んで火傷をし病み苦しんでいるときに、その嘔吐物（たぐり）から化生した神である。

claims.statement: A Nihon Shoki variant mentions only Kanayamahiko in this birth episode.
claims.statement_id: Versi alternatif Nihon Shoki hanya menyebut Kanayamahiko dalam peristiwa kelahiran ini.
claims.quote: 『古事記』では金山毘古神・金山毘売神の二神、『日本書紀』の第三の一書では金山彦神のみが化生している。

claims.statement: Katawaguruma is a Japanese yōkai from old supernatural tales.
claims.statement_id: Katawaguruma adalah yōkai Jepang dari cerita gaib lama.
claims.quote: 片輪車（かたわぐるま）は、江戸時代の怪談などの古書に見られる日本の妖怪。炎に包まれた片輪のみの牛車が美女または恐ろしい男を乗せて走り、姿を見たものを祟るとされる。

claims.statement: It takes the form of a flaming single-wheeled cart bearing a woman or frightening man.
claims.statement_id: Wujudnya kereta beroda tunggal yang terbakar dan membawa perempuan atau laki-laki menakutkan.
claims.quote: 片輪車（かたわぐるま）は、江戸時代の怪談などの古書に見られる日本の妖怪。炎に包まれた片輪のみの牛車が美女または恐ろしい男を乗せて走り、姿を見たものを祟るとされる。

claims.statement: An account says it curses people who see it.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah menyebut ia mengutuk orang yang melihatnya.
claims.quote: These demons bestow powerful curses on any who see them.

claims.statement: A Shiga tale describes the abduction of a curious woman’s child.
claims.statement_id: Cerita Shiga menggambarkan penculikan anak dari seorang perempuan yang mengintipnya.
claims.quote: In a 17th century record, when a katawaguruma attacked a village in what is now Shiga, she abducted the child of a woman who dared to peek at her through a crack in her door, saying “Instead of watching me you should have been watching your child!”

claims.statement: That tale ends with the child being returned after the mother’s remorse.
claims.statement_id: Cerita tersebut berakhir dengan anak dikembalikan setelah ibunya menyesal.
claims.quote: The next night, the katawaguruma came again and saw that the woman was truly regretful. She returned the child unharmed.

claims.statement: It is said never to appear in that village again.
claims.statement_id: Ia konon tidak pernah muncul lagi di desa itu.
claims.quote: The katawaguruma was never seen in that village again.

claims.statement: An Edo-period card depicts a male form based on Shokoku Hyaku Monogatari.
claims.statement_id: Kartu zaman Edo menggambar wujud laki-laki berdasarkan Shokoku Hyaku Monogatari.
claims.quote: 江戸時代の妖怪かるた「京の町へ出るかたわ車」の絵札にある片輪車は『諸国百物語』に基づき、男性の姿で描かれている。

claims.statement: Sekien’s illustrated collection instead depicts a female form.
claims.statement_id: Kumpulan ilustrasi Sekien justru menggambar wujud perempuan.
claims.quote: 対して鳥山石燕の画集『今昔画図続百鬼』では『諸国里人談』に記述に基いて女性の姿であり

claims.statement: Kawaakago is a Japanese yōkai depicted as a baby near water.
claims.statement_id: Kawaakago adalah yōkai Jepang yang digambar sebagai bayi di dekat air.
claims.quote: 川赤子（かわあかご）は、鳥山石燕の妖怪画集『今昔画図続百鬼』にある日本の妖怪。その名の通り、川、沼、池などの水辺に出現する、赤ん坊の姿の妖怪とされる。

claims.statement: Sekien’s illustration shows its upper body beside riverside reeds.
claims.statement_id: Ilustrasi Sekien menunjukkan bagian atas tubuhnya di dekat buluh tepi sungai.
claims.quote: 『今昔画図続百鬼』によれば、葦の葉の茂った川辺から上半身のみ姿を現した様子が描かれており、川童（=河童）の一種との解説文が添えられている。

claims.statement: A later account gives it the appearance of a small red-skinned baby.
claims.statement_id: Kisah belakangan memberinya penampilan bayi kecil berkulit merah.
claims.quote: They look like small, red-skinned babies.

claims.statement: That account says it imitates a baby’s crying to attract passersby.
claims.statement_id: Kisah itu menyebut ia meniru tangisan bayi untuk menarik orang yang lewat.
claims.quote: Kawa akago appear on riverbanks and call out to passersby, perfectly mimicking the sound of crying human babies: “Waah! Waah!” (Japanese: “ Ogyaa! Ogyaa! ”)

claims.statement: The later story warns that its prank can end in drowning.
claims.statement_id: Cerita belakangan menyebut leluconnya dapat berakhir dengan orang tenggelam.
claims.quote: While this is only meant as a prank, some people drown in this manner.

claims.statement: One scholarly interpretation regards the image as wordplay rather than a recorded folk creature.
claims.statement_id: Satu tafsir peneliti menganggap gambar itu sebagai permainan kata, bukan makhluk yang tercatat dalam tradisi rakyat.
claims.quote: また妖怪研究家・多田克己は、同画図の川赤子の背景にはいかだと釣竿が描かれており、イトミミズが赤子と呼ばれていたことから、実際に伝承されている妖怪を描いたものではなく、一種の洒落で描かれたものとの説を唱えている。

claims.statement: Kechibi is a ghost light in Kōchi folklore.
claims.statement_id: Kechibi adalah cahaya gaib dalam cerita rakyat Kōchi.
claims.quote: Kechibi (けち火) is an atmospheric ghost light told in the legends of Kōchi Prefecture.

claims.statement: One account interprets it as a human spirit turned into fire.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah menafsirkannya sebagai roh manusia yang berubah menjadi api.
claims.quote: It is stated to be the onryō of humans turned into balls of fire, and it is said to be possible to beckon for it by beating a zōri three times, or putting saliva on the zōri and calling for it.

claims.statement: A human face is said to float within the flames.
claims.statement_id: Wajah manusia konon mengambang di dalam nyalanya.
claims.quote: It is also said that the face of a human floats in the fire.

claims.statement: Its appearance above water links it with ship ghosts in some accounts.
claims.statement_id: Kemunculannya di atas air menghubungkannya dengan hantu kapal dalam beberapa kisah.
claims.quote: They are also said to appear above water, and from this they are sometimes called a type of funayūrei.

claims.statement: Other accounts distinguish sleeping people’s spirits from souls unable to move on.
claims.statement_id: Kisah lain membedakan roh orang yang tidur dari arwah yang tidak dapat melanjutkan ke alam berikutnya.
claims.quote: There are two types of kechibi: those that come out of living humans while they sleep, and those which appear when a soul cannot move on to the next life properly.

claims.statement: The figure appears in an Edo-period illustrated scroll.
claims.statement_id: Sosok itu muncul dalam gulungan bergambar zaman Edo.
claims.quote: They appear in Tōsa obake zōshi , a yōkai picture scroll from the Edo period.

claims.statement: Keukegen is a creature illustrated by Toriyama Sekien.
claims.statement_id: Keukegen adalah makhluk yang digambar oleh Toriyama Sekien.
claims.quote: Keukegen (毛羽毛現; "fluffy hair appearance") is a creature illustrated in Toriyama Sekien's Konjaku Hyakki Shūi.

claims.statement: It resembles a small dog covered in long hair.
claims.statement_id: Ia menyerupai anjing kecil yang tertutup rambut panjang.
claims.quote: It resembles a small dog covered entirely in long hair.

claims.statement: Its name also forms a pun meaning a rarely seen unusual thing.
claims.statement_id: Namanya juga menjadi permainan kata yang berarti sesuatu yang aneh dan jarang terlihat.
claims.quote: Its name is a pun - when written with different kanji (希有怪訝), keukegen means "an unusual thing which is rarely seen".

claims.statement: One account describes it as a disease spirit in damp, dark places.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah menggambarkannya sebagai roh penyakit di tempat lembap dan gelap.
claims.quote: According to one report, the keukegen is a disease spirit which lives in damp, dark places and causes people in the house to get sick.

claims.statement: A reference also associates it with bad luck.
claims.statement_id: Satu rujukan juga mengaitkannya dengan nasib buruk.
claims.quote: They are actually a kind of minor spirit of bad luck, disease, and pestilence.

claims.statement: It is portrayed as shy and avoiding human contact.
claims.statement_id: Ia digambarkan pemalu dan menghindari kontak dengan manusia.
claims.quote: Being shy by nature, they try to avoid human contact and are rarely seen.

claims.statement: Kidōmaru is an oni in the Kamakura-period Kokon Chomonjū.
claims.statement_id: Kidōmaru adalah oni dalam Kokon Chomonjū dari zaman Kamakura.
claims.quote: Kidōmaru (鬼童丸, 鬼同丸) is an oni that appears in the Kamakura period collection of setsuwa, the Kokon Chomonjū, among other sources.

claims.statement: A tale has Yorimitsu order him restrained with chains.
claims.statement_id: Satu cerita menyebut Yorimitsu memerintahkan agar ia diikat dengan rantai.
claims.quote: Yorimitsu said that Yorinobu was careless, so they should restrain the oni with chains, and stayed at Yorinobu's house for that night.

claims.statement: He breaks the chains and bears a grudge against Yorimitsu.
claims.statement_id: Ia memutus rantai dan menyimpan dendam terhadap Yorimitsu.
claims.quote: Kidōmaru easily tore off those chains, and with a grudge against Yorimitsu, looked at his bed and kept watch.

claims.statement: He hides inside a slain cow while waiting to ambush Yorimitsu.
claims.statement_id: Ia bersembunyi di dalam sapi yang dibunuh sambil menunggu untuk menyergap Yorimitsu.
claims.quote: Yorimitsu noticed this and told a servant, "tomorrow, I will make a visit to the Kurama temple." Kidōmaru then went ahead to Kurama, killed one free-ranging cattle at the Ichihara field, hid inside its body, and waited for Yorimitsu to come.

claims.statement: The encounter ends with Yorimitsu killing him.
claims.statement_id: Pertemuan itu berakhir dengan Yorimitsu membunuhnya.
claims.quote: It is said that Kidōmaru appeared from inside the cow and tried to slash at Yorimitsu, but Yorimitsu struck down Kidōmaru with a single strike.

claims.statement: Sekien depicts him wearing a cow’s hide in the snow.
claims.statement_id: Sekien menggambarnya memakai kulit sapi di tengah salju.
claims.quote: In the yōkai pictures collection, the Konjaku Hyakki Shūi by Toriyama Sekien, under the title of "Kidō," it depicts Kidōmaru in the snow wearing the skin of a cattle waiting for Yorimitsu to come.

claims.statement: Kinoko are yōkai in legends of the Kinki region.
claims.statement_id: Kinoko adalah yōkai dalam legenda wilayah Kinki.
claims.quote: The kinoko (木の子) is a yōkai told in legends of the Kinki region.

claims.statement: Some traditions place them in mountains and relate them to yamawaro.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian tradisi menempatkan mereka di pegunungan dan menghubungkannya dengan yamawaro.
claims.quote: In the Yoshino region of Nara Prefecture and in Hyōgo Prefecture, they are yōkai said to be in mountainous regions and are a type of the mountain yōkai yamawaro.

claims.statement: They resemble young children dressed in leaves or blue clothing.
claims.statement_id: Mereka menyerupai anak kecil berpakaian daun atau pakaian biru.
claims.quote: They appear as children from two to four years of age and wear clothes that are made of leaves or are blue.

claims.statement: Their shadow-like appearance makes them difficult to perceive.
claims.statement_id: Penampilannya yang seperti bayangan membuat mereka sulit dikenali.
claims.quote: It's said that when a human sees one, they look like a shadow, making it hard to tell if one is actually there or not.

claims.statement: They are said to play together in groups.
claims.statement_id: Mereka konon bermain bersama dalam kelompok.
claims.quote: They usually play together as a group.

claims.statement: Woodcutters are said to encounter them from time to time.
claims.statement_id: Penebang kayu konon sesekali menjumpai mereka.
claims.quote: It is said that woodcutters and other people who work in the mountains catch sight of them from time to time and so they are not an unusual sight to them.

claims.statement: Konpira Gongen is a Japanese deity associated with Shugendō and Kotohira.
claims.statement_id: Konpira Gongen adalah dewa Jepang yang dikaitkan dengan Shugendō dan Kotohira.
claims.quote: Konpira Gongen (金毘羅権現) is a Japanese god of the Shugendō sect originating in the mountain Kotohira of Kagawa Prefecture.

claims.statement: He is regarded as a deity of merchant sailors.
claims.statement_id: Ia dianggap sebagai dewa pelaut niaga.
claims.quote: He is the god of merchant sailors.

claims.statement: A legend connects his origin with the summoning of Kumbhīra at Matsuo Temple.
claims.statement_id: Satu legenda menghubungkan asalnya dengan pemanggilan Kumbhīra di Kuil Matsuo.
claims.quote: According to legend Konpira Gongen came into existence when a priest at Matsuo Temple ... summoned the Ganges deity Kumbhīra

claims.statement: Kumbhīra is described as a crocodile deity of the Ganges.
claims.statement_id: Kumbhīra digambarkan sebagai dewa buaya Sungai Gangga.
claims.quote: He is a Ganges crocodile god. He is identified with the first of the twelve spirit messengers emanating from Bhaisajyaguru.

claims.statement: The figure is associated with the twelve spirit messengers of Bhaisajyaguru.
claims.statement_id: Sosok itu dikaitkan dengan dua belas utusan roh Bhaisajyaguru.
claims.quote: He is identified with the first of the twelve spirit messengers emanating from Bhaisajyaguru.

claims.statement: Japanese worship came to portray Konpira as a guardian of Buddhism.
claims.statement_id: Pemujaan di Jepang kemudian menggambarkan Konpira sebagai pelindung agama Buddha.
claims.quote: As time passed, people in Japan began to see Konpira as a guardian of their Buddhist religion.
